title: Can you really do two things at once?
hook: Multitasking feels efficient, but every switch has a price.
summary: Mostly not: the mind isn’t built for heavy multitasking, and every switch between tasks costs time and accuracy.

cardBlocks.text: Multitasking can mean doing two tasks at the same time, switching between them, or doing them in quick succession. Psychologists who study it have concluded that the mind and brain were not designed for heavy-duty multitasking. In task-switching experiments, people lost time whenever they had to move from one task to another, and the more complex the tasks, the more time they lost.

Each switch costs only a few tenths of a second, but the cost adds up when people go back and forth many times. According to psychologist David Meyer, these brief mental blocks can eat up as much as 40% of someone’s productive time. Multitasking may look efficient, but it can end up taking longer and producing more errors.
Every task switch costs time; added up, switching makes multitasking slower and more error-prone.

deepDiveBlocks.text: According to Meyer and colleagues, the brain’s executive control works in two stages: goal shifting ("I want to do this now instead of that") and rule activation ("I’m turning off the rules for that and turning on the rules for this").
Even when the switch is predictable
In the 1990s, Robert Rogers and Stephen Monsell showed that even when people knew exactly when they would switch tasks, they were slower on a switch than when repeating the same task.

Losing half a second to a task switch can make a life-or-death difference for a driver on a phone. In that time the car can travel far enough to hit an obstacle that could otherwise have been avoided.
